tldr: Using reinforcement learning relying solely on the robot's own joint encoder history—without any cameras, force/torque, or tactile sensors—this work accomplishes peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading with tight clearances of 0.5 to 1.5 mm. A peg insertion policy trained purely in simulation transfers zero-shot to a real robot without fine-tuning, achieving a 73% success rate across diverse parts including unseen shapes.
hero_caption: A real robot performing peg insertion without vision, relying only on its joint encoders and past action history. Even without knowing the hole's location or the grasp misalignment, it explores via contact by tracing the surface, finds the opening, and smoothly seats the part.
overview:
In robotic precision assembly, relying on in-hand cameras for visual feedback, wrist force/torque (F/T) sensors, or expensive tactile sensors has long been standard practice. However, just as legged robots and humanoids traverse rough terrain using only joint motion, the encoders in a robot's arm joints can also serve as very high-resolution contact sensors. The challenge has been that, unlike the large impact forces in locomotion, contact forces in precision assembly are tiny and easily buried in joint deflections and minute displacements.

To tackle this, the authors completely cut off external visual, force, and tactile sensors. They trained "blind assembly policies" via reinforcement learning that take only a 0.6-second history of joint positions, velocities, and past actions as input. Neither the fixture's pose nor the part's grasp pose inside the gripper is provided. The policy must discover alignment entirely through contact. To make this learning possible, the authors developed "mjfit," a custom procedural model generator that maintains precise contact clearances while enabling fast simulation. They trained across diverse part shapes in over 10,000 parallel simulation environments.

As a result, the policy successfully learned not only peg insertion but also highly contact-rich tasks like gear meshing and nut threading onto bolts, all using proprioception alone. Furthermore, when the simulation-trained policy was deployed directly onto a real robot arm, it achieved a 73% zero-shot success rate across pegs of unseen shapes, sizes, and tighter clearances. Remarkably, the blind policy exhibited far superior generalization to unseen part shapes compared to vision-based policies, which tend to be easily distracted by visual appearance.
contributions: Developed reinforcement learning policies that achieve precision peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading using only joint encoder histories, without visual, force/torque, or tactile sensing, or fixture pose information.
Demonstrated that a blind policy trained purely in simulation transfers zero-shot to a real robot arm (Flexiv Rizon 4S), inserting pegs of diverse and unseen shapes with a 73% success rate.
Analyzed the learned latent representations using linear probes, proving the policy does not run a fixed script but accurately identifies contact modes to adaptively switch its search behaviors.
Showed that because actions are driven by contact, the blind policy generalizes to unseen shapes and sizes far better than an in-hand visual policy.

Developed and released "mjfit," an open-source procedural generator that rapidly builds thousands of assembly assets for MuJoCo from exact convex pieces while strictly preserving sub-millimeter clearances.

sections.heading: Can a robot's own joints act as high-resolution contact sensors?
sections.summary: External forces on an arm translate into joint displacements through its links, turning every joint encoder into a contact sensor. This work proposes blind policies that solve sub-millimeter precision assembly using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Trained purely in simulation, the policy transfers zero-shot to a real robot and achieves high success on unseen parts.
sections.details:
Whenever a robot touches something, the resulting force travels through its links to the joints. This creates tiny discrepancies between commanded and actual joint states. In other words, a robot's joint encoders inherently function as whole-body contact sensors. Legged robots and humanoids already exploit this proprioception—the internal sense of joint positions and velocities—to walk blindly. However, contact forces during walking are large and relatively easy to detect.

Precision assembly with robot arms sits at the opposite extreme. Finding millimeter-scale openings, meshing gear teeth, and catching screw threads require sensing very light contacts. This leads directly to the core question of the paper: is joint sensing really enough for millimeter-scale precision assembly?

To find out, the authors randomized part shapes, fixture poses, and the in-gripper grasp poses. They trained RL policies that operate on just a 0.6-second history of joint states without cameras or force sensors. The policies achieved near-perfect success across three challenging tasks: peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. In real-world experiments, the peg insertion policy achieved a 73% zero-shot success rate across eight peg variants, including shapes outside the training distribution.

Analyzing the learned internal representations revealed something fascinating: the robot does not simply execute a hard-coded pattern like a spiral search. Instead, it accurately perceives its contact state and dynamically adapts its behavior. Moreover, because it does not rely on vision, the blind policy proved substantially more robust to unseen part appearances than visual baselines.

captions.F1: Photo sequence of peg insertion on the real robot. Using only joint encoder information, it adaptively progresses through contact, search, capture, and fully seated states.

sections.heading: How do exact simulation and auxiliary contact losses enable blind learning?
sections.summary: The authors formulated three contact-rich tasks—peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading—generating thousands of variations for reinforcement learning. They developed "mjfit" to procedurally decompose shapes into exact convex pieces without sacrificing clearance. Adding an auxiliary contact prediction loss during training enabled efficient learning without vision.
sections.details:
### 2.1 The Three Assembly Tasks
The authors studied three tasks: peg insertion, spur gear meshing, and nut threading. All setups use a 7-DoF arm with a parallel-jaw gripper. Fixture poses and grasp misalignments are heavily randomized and completely unknown to the policy.
- Peg Insertion: Clearance of 1.0 to 1.5 mm per side. The peg makes contact roughly 2 cm away from the hole and must correct its tilt to insert.
- Gear Meshing: Backlash between gear teeth of 0.2 to 0.6 mm. Starting in contact with the shaft tip, the gear must phase-align its teeth with another fixed gear and slide down.
- Nut Threading: Thread clearance of just 0.05 to 0.2 mm. Targeting M24 to M42 metric threads, the nut starts at the bolt tip and must engage the threads and screw down.

### 2.2 Developing the mjfit Simulator Asset Generator
Simulating such tight clearances in MuJoCo at scale posed a problem for existing convex decomposition tools like CoACD and V-HACD. These tools often intrude extra geometry into concavities, accidentally filling the designed clearance. Signed Distance Field (SDF) collision detection was computationally heavy and tended to round sharp edges, causing missed contacts.
To solve this, the authors created "mjfit," which automatically generates and combines exact convex prisms from arbitrary 2D profiles. It produces assets that strictly maintain exact geometric clearances. This allowed 12,288 parallel simulation environments to run distinct assembly shapes at high speed without collision artifacts.

### 2.3 Policy Architecture and Auxiliary Contact Loss
The actor network takes the past 0.6 seconds (30 steps) of joint positions, velocities, end-effector poses, velocities, and previous actions as input. It receives no camera images, external force measurements, or target hole poses. A temporal convolution layer compresses this history into a 32-dimensional latent vector $z_t$. An MLP then outputs delta joint position commands, tracked by a joint impedance controller.
The policy is trained with PPO. Without vision, identifying contact is hard and slows training. To accelerate learning, the authors introduced an auxiliary contact loss during training only. Using privileged simulator data, surface sample points are labeled as free, in-contact, or engaged. A small auxiliary decoder learns to predict these contact states from $z_t$. This gradient guides the temporal encoder to capture contact-relevant features much faster. The decoder is discarded during real-world deployment, preventing any privileged data leakage.

sections.heading: Why is a blind policy more robust than looking with cameras?
sections.summary: The proprioceptive policy matched the near-100% success rate of an eye-in-hand visual policy. Latent representation analysis proved that the policy accurately identifies contact modes and adapts its motion. On unseen shapes, the blind policy generalized far better than the visual policy, which struggled with changed visual appearances.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Can Assembly Succeed on Joint Sensing Alone?
In training curves, the blind policy reached nearly 100% success across peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading, matching an eye-in-hand RGB visual policy. Peg insertion took slightly longer because the robot had to search the surface for the opening. However, in gear meshing and threading, the parts themselves occlude the view, meaning both blind and visual policies finished in nearly identical times.

### 3.2 Is It Truly Adaptive or Just a Fixed Pattern?
To confirm the policy was not simply running a fixed spiral search, the authors evaluated the latent vector $z_t$ using linear probes. When classifying the task state into seven distinct modes (e.g., free space, distant search, captured at opening, seated), a single-frame observation achieved only ~60% accuracy. In contrast, the history-compressed latent $z_t$ decoded the mode with over 70% accuracy.
Furthermore, swapping latent representations from different modes during execution (Latent-swap) caused immediate, drastic shifts in the output actions. This confirms that the policy reads its current contact state from $z_t$ and dynamically alters its behavior. Compared to an industry-standard spiral baseline that traveled an average of 95 mm, the policy detected the opening upon catching the edge and corrected course, finding the hole with a median travel of only 37 mm.

### 3.3 Generalization to Unseen Shapes
Testing on part geometries and sizes not seen during training revealed a striking difference. Visual policies suffered sharp performance drops because visual feature alignment degraded under appearance changes. In contrast, the blind policy's strategy—sliding along the surface and driving downward upon catching an edge—held up regardless of shape. This highlights a key takeaway: proprioception is far less susceptible to visual domain gaps when geometry shifts.

### 3.4 Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer
The simulation-trained peg insertion policy was deployed directly to a real robot arm (Flexiv Rizon 4S) without additional training. It achieved 73% to 80% success on in-distribution pegs. It also maintained strong performance on out-of-distribution pegs: 66% on a tighter 0.5 mm clearance peg, 66% on a large-area cross-section peg, and 72% on a long peg. Overall, it succeeded in 173 out of 237 trials (73%).

sections.heading: How does this shift the paradigm from force sensors and cameras?
sections.summary: Prior precision insertion research relied heavily on F/T sensors, high-density tactile arrays, or visual fusion. This work imports temporal proprioceptive processing from legged robotics into manipulation, achieving millimeter-precision assembly without external sensors.
sections.details:
Robotic peg insertion has a long history. Classical methods combined compliance mechanisms with heuristic search patterns like spirals. However, these systems assumed known grasping poses and required careful manual tuning for each part.

Recent learning-based approaches typically rely on wrist-mounted force/torque (F/T) sensors, eye-in-hand cameras, or expensive fingertip tactile arrays. These setups have demonstrated success in compensating for position errors of a few millimeters.

Meanwhile, legged robotics has achieved great success traversing rough terrain without vision, relying entirely on joint encoder histories. This work adapts that concept of temporal proprioceptive representations to precision manipulation. It is the first to demonstrate millimeter to sub-millimeter assembly without external sensors under large grasp and fixture uncertainties.

From a simulation perspective, the work also addresses long-standing challenges in simulating micro-clearances. It provides a procedural generation pipeline that avoids the penetration and rounding errors common in SDFs and standard convex decomposition methods.

sections.heading: What are the current limitations and future directions?
sections.summary: While joint sensing alone enables high-precision assembly, this method functions primarily as a "last-mile" skill after contact occurs. Future work must address initial coarse approach motions and recovery from catastrophic grasp slips.
sections.details:
This study proves that robot joint sensing alone can solve challenging assembly tasks like peg insertion, gear meshing, and threading. Nonetheless, the authors note several clear limitations.

The most important constraint is that this is a "last-mile" skill. Every training episode begins with the part already in contact within a few centimeters of the fixture. Coarse guidance—picking a part from a bin and bringing it close to the opening—still requires vision or pre-planned trajectories.

In addition, the learned search behavior is local. If the peg slips drastically inside the gripper fingers or falls far from the opening, the policy cannot recover on its own to restart the search. Building a hybrid system that smoothly hands off from a global visual policy to this local blind policy is an exciting next step.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and ablation studies
sections.summary: This section covers how the contact auxiliary loss speeds up learning by up to 5x, safety torque penalties for real-world deployment, and detailed simulator collision benchmarks.
sections.details:
### Auxiliary Contact Loss Ablation
Without the auxiliary contact loss, the policy still eventually solves all three tasks. However, reaching a 90% success rate required 2.7x more environment steps for peg insertion, 3.8x more for gear meshing, and 5.1x more for nut threading. Guiding the latent representation with contact states clearly provides a massive learning speedup for blind policies.

### Deployment on the Real Robot
For transfer to the Flexiv Rizon 4S arm, safety penalties were added to protect hardware. After initial task learning, an additional training phase penalized joint velocities and commanded torques exceeding one-sixth of hardware limits. This ensured smooth, safe surface-sweeping motions on the physical hardware.

### Details of the mjfit Benchmark
In collision benchmarks across hole clearances from 20 µm to 200 µm, baseline methods (CoACD and V-HACD) introduced interior mesh artifacts due to decomposition tolerances, causing pegs to jam. Because mjfit constructs geometry via exact convex polygon extrusions, it fully preserves designed clearances. It achieved the best Pareto frontier for CPU and GPU speeds with zero geometric intrusion error (chordal error only).

takeaways: Joint encoder temporal histories contain sufficient signal to resolve sub-millimeter contact states.
Blind policies generalize better to unseen shapes and sizes than visual policies because they are unaffected by visual appearance changes.
Sim-to-real transfer for tight assembly requires simulation geometry that strictly preserves clearances, such as mjfit's exact convex pieces.
Supervising latent representations with privileged contact states speeds up reinforcement learning for sparse-reward contact search by several times.
limitations: The policy is restricted to local exploration (the last mile) after contact, requiring external guidance to bring parts near the opening.
It cannot recover from catastrophic failures, such as parts dropping or slipping heavily inside the gripper beyond training limits.
Accurate robot system identification, including joint impedance parameters, friction, and damping, is required.
